description: The Journal of Global Research in Multidisciplinary Studies (JGRMS) publishes peer-reviewed research across diverse disciplines, promoting global knowledge exchange.

The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.

Abstract
The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.

II. PHISHING ATTACKS DETECTION TECHNIQUES 
Phishing attacks, a type of cybersecurity threat related to 
network attacks, pose as reputable companies or people to 
coerce victims into disclosing personal information[9][10]. 
This technique entails contacting a large number of people at 
random with phony emails, phone calls, or SMS messages 
asking them to divulge their private information. They pretend 
to be from a reputable organization or entity in order to 
defraud individuals of their password and other personal 
information. From a direct message to a fake website, 
whatever share ends up in a scammer's pocket and may be 
used. 
A. Types of Phishing Attacks 
There are two types of phishing attacks depending on the 
communication method and the cybercriminal attack method. 
Usual examples are spear phishing, whaling and vishing 
(voice phishing). Each kind aims to deceive the user into 
disclosing personal information, such as login credentials, 
financial information, or personal details, by posing as a 
reliable person or organization. The increasingly sophisticated 
nature of phishing attacks calls for sophisticated methods of 
detection and user awareness, otherwise the risk of successful 
attacks increases. 
1) Deceptive Phishing 
This is the most prevalent kind of phishing, when the 
attackers pretend to be a reputable business in an attempt to 
get people's login credentials or personal information.  The 
users are subsequently coerced into complying with the 
hacker's demands. 
2) Spear Phishing 
An intrusion detection and prevention system that is based 
on wireless technology examines wireless protocol behaviors 
in order to identify potential threats and implements 
countermeasures.  It can identify if someone is using an illegal 
wireless local area network [5].  Application, transport, and 
protocol layer suspicious behavior cannot be detected. 
3) Clone Phishing 
This kind of phishing attempt involves using an already-
existing email with the same or similar attachments and links, 
as well as the recipient's address book, to craft a new email. A 
malicious version of the attachment or link inside the email is 
delivered to the victim using an email address that is spoofing 
to make it look to have originated from the original sender. 
4) Whaling 
This is one kind of phishing; in it, the perpetrator targets 
the victim's high social standing in an effort to get access to 
sensitive information through various online platforms, such 
as social media accounts. 
5) Link Manipulation 
Phishing techniques include "Link Manipulation," in 
which the perpetrator spoofs or otherwise compromises a 
target's website by sending a link to it. In reality, rather of 
directing the visitor to the advertised website, clicking on that 
link actually accesses the phisher's website.Voice 
PhishingThe term "voice phishing" describes a specific type 
of phone criminal assault in which the perpetrator uses social 
engineering techniques in conjunction with the telephone 
network to get access to victims' sensitive financial and 
personal data.  
B. Phishing attack Lifecycle 
The phishing attack lifecycle is a series of steps that 
attackers take to target individuals, create a phishing kit, send 
a scam message, deceive the user into clicking on a link, and 
remove evidence. Recognizing these stages helps in detecting, 
preventing, and mitigating phishing attacks effectively. A 
typical phishing attempt goes through several stages, as 
illustrated in Fig. 1 below [11].

D. Traditional Phishing Detection Techniques  
Phishing detection methods are based on rules, blacklists, 
whitelists, signatures and heuristic analysis of phishing web 
sites and e-mails. These methods are effective for detecting 
known phishing attacks and require relatively low 
computational resources. However, they have limited 
capability in detecting new or evolving phishing attacks, 
making them less effective against zero-day threats. 
1) List-Based Detection Techniques 
In order to shield the user from an online phishing scam, 
list-based detection evaluates the URL's validity using lists. 
According to this method, a list is kept as a database of URLs. 
There are often URLs, IP addresses, and keywords stored 
there. A whitelist, consisting of links to valid websites, is kept 
by certain researchers. 
2) Heuristic Rule-Based Detection Techniques 
The suspicious URL is subject to thumb rules used by 
heuristic rule-based detection systems in order to ensure 
security. Most of the time, there are such few changes between 
real and phishing site addresses that users are unable to tell 
them apart [18]. Criminals put a lot of effort into creating fake 
websites so that people won't believe they're real. 
3) Signature-Based Detection Techniques 
An intrusion detection system's signature-based detection 
mechanism looks for suspicious behavior by comparing 
incoming network traffic to a database of previously identified 
attack signatures [19]. Each signature corresponds to a 
specific type of threat, capturing its unique characteristics.

PROCESSING BASED PHISHING DETECTION 
ML is a subfield of AI concerned with developing systems 
and algorithms that can autonomously learn from data, 
generate predictions, and make judgments [20]. Large datasets 
are used to train ML algorithms [21]. used for phishing 
identification, it incorporates characteristics from both 
popular phishing sites and legal ones. In order to accurately 
categorize questionable websites, these algorithms learn to 
spot patterns, outliers, and telltale indicators of phishing 
attempts. 
1) Supervised Learning  
In order to train a classification model that can assign each 
input data point to one of a predetermined number of classes, 
supervised ML algorithms need massive labeled datasets as 
resources [22]. A ML pipeline for training supervised models 
to identify phishing attempts. As there are just two possible 
outcomes in a phishing webpage detection problem—
phishing or benign—the trained models are binary classifiers. 
2) Unsupervised Learning 
Unsupervised learning is used when data is only provided 
as an input and there is no corresponding output variable. Such 
algorithms model the underlying patterns in the data to learn 
more about its properties. 
3) Semi-supervised Learning 
This is a cross between supervised and unsupervised 
learning methods [23]. These algorithms are trained on a 
combination of labeled and unlabeled data. In a typical 
context, there is a small amount of labeled data and a big 
number of unlabeled data. 
4) Reinforcement Learning 
RL is used when the objective at hand is to make a series 
of decisions leading to a final reward. During the learning 
process, an artificial agent is rewarded or penalized for acts it 
takes. The aim is to maximize the overall prize. Examples 
include teaching agents to play computer games or doing 
robotics tasks with an end objective. 
B. Emerging Machine Learning Algorithms for Phishing 
Detection  
Emerging ML algorithms have significantly improved 
phishing detection by learning complex patterns from URLs, 
emails, and website content. Ensemble learning, GNNs, 
transformers, and XAI are among the advanced techniques 
that deliver greater accuracy in phishing detection, 
adaptability to new phishing tactics, and a lower false positive 
rate. The algorithms facilitate the identification of 
sophisticated and never-observed phishing attacks in real 
time.

LR is one of the most used ML algorithms for binary 
classification. This is because it is a basic calculation that 
performs very well on a wide scope of issues. The logistic

information and makes an estimate of the likelihood that the 
information belongs to the default class. 
2) K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) 
Predictions for another event (x) are generated using the 
whole training set for the K most relevant models (neighbors), 
and the output variable for those K events is summarized. This 
might be the mean output variable in regression, or it could be 
the median class value in characterization. A distance metric 
is used to determine which of the K examples in the test 
dataset are the most similar to each other.

V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK 
Phishing attacks are still becoming more sophisticated, 
making them a threat to individuals, organizations and 
cybersecurity systems. This review considers the development 
of phishing attacks, the traditional phishing detection 
methods, and the latest developments in intelligent phishing 
detection. Blacklist-, whitelist-, heuristic-, rule- and signature-
based solutions are still valuable but not very effective to 
identify emerging and zero-day phishing attacks. The 
classification accuracy of the ML algorithms such as LR, DT, 
RF, SVM, NB, and KNN has been found to be improved 
through learning discriminative patterns in phishing datasets. 
Furthermore, DL models, such as ANNs, CNNs, RNNs, and 
LSTM networks, provide enhanced capability for automatic 
feature extraction and detection of complex phishing 
behaviors. NLP techniques enhance phishing detection by 
leveraging textual analysis, semantic relationships within 
emails and web pages, and social engineering indicators. 
The creation of real-time zero-day phishing attack 
detectors that are lightweight, explainable, and adaptable 
requires more research. Integrating transformer-based 
architectures, XAI, federated learning, and multimodal 
analysis can further improve detection accuracy, scalability, 
privacy preservation, and robustness against rapidly evolving 
phishing techniques.

GENERATIVE AI AND CRIMINAL LIABILITY: DEEPFAKE-ENABLED 
FRAUD AND ATTRIBUTION IN 2026 
Sergio Pommier Gallo, PhD. 
ORCID iD: 0009-0000-7387-3943 
Affiliation: Stanford University 
Website: https://sergiopommiergallophd.blogspot.com 
 
Abstract 
This study examines the emergence of generative artificial intelligence as a structural 
enabler of deepfake-based fraud and extortion within contemporary criminal systems. 
Moving beyond traditional evidentiary paradigms, the research analyzes how synthetic 
media disrupts attribution, evidentiary reliability, and doctrinal interpretations of mens 
rea. Using an interdisciplinary framework integrating criminal law, digital forensics, 
and criminological analysis, the study identifies patterns of deception, operational 
scalability, and attribution ambiguity. The findings support the hypothesis that 
generative AI functions as an evidentiary distortion mechanism that complicates, but 
does not eliminate, individual criminal responsibility. The article proposes a doctrinal 
model of algorithmic attribution that distinguishes between synthetic output and human 
agency, reinforcing evidentiary safeguards necessary for due process in technologically 
mediated criminal environments. 
Keywords: artificial intelligence; deepfakes; criminal liability; digital evidence; 
attribution; fraud; cybercrime. 
 
1. Introduction 
The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has introduced a new 
paradigm in the production of synthetic audiovisual content. By 2026, deepfake 
technologies have evolved from experimental tools into operational instruments 
used in fraud, extortion, reputational attacks, and financial deception. These 
technologies enable the fabrication of highly convincing representations of 
individuals, including voice cloning and real-time video manipulation, thereby 
significantly expanding the operational capabilities of criminal actors. 
Traditional criminal law frameworks are grounded in assumptions of evidentiary 
stability and identifiable authorship. However, deepfake technologies undermine these 
assumptions by decoupling observable evidence from verifiable human conduct. This 
creates a critical tension between technological capability and doctrinal requirements 
for attribution and intent. 
Research Question: How does generative AI-based synthetic media affect attribution, 
evidentiary reliability, and criminal liability in contemporary legal systems? 
Hypothesis (H1): Deepfake-enabled criminal conduct introduces structural distortions in 
evidentiary evaluation, requiring enhanced doctrinal safeguards without altering the 
foundational principles of individual culpability. 
 
2. Theoretical Framework 
This study integrates criminal law doctrine with theories of technological 
mediation, digital deception, and evidentiary reliability. 
The concept of synthetic evidence is defined as digitally generated content that 
simulates reality without direct correspondence to actual events. Unlike manipulated 
evidence, synthetic evidence may be entirely fabricated without any original referent. 
Algorithmic attribution is introduced as a doctrinal concept referring to the process of 
linking human intent and agency to outcomes generated or mediated by artificial 
systems. 
The framework distinguishes three layers: 
(1) generation (algorithmic creation), 
(2) deployment (human use and dissemination), 
(3) intent (criminal purpose). 
This layered model preserves the centrality of human agency while recognizing the 
mediating role of technology. 
 
3. Methodology 
The study employs a qualitative doctrinal and criminological methodology. 
Data sources include: legal scholarship; cybercrime reports; forensic analysis literature; 
documented case patterns; and interdisciplinary research on AI and law. 
Analytical approach: doctrinal analysis combined with criminological pattern 
recognition and forensic reasoning. 
Variables analyzed: attribution complexity; evidentiary reliability; intent inference; 
technological mediation; procedural safeguards. 
Evidence classification: 
High = peer-reviewed legal and scientific literature 
Medium = institutional reports and documented case patterns 
Inferential = doctrinal synthesis and criminological inference 
 
4. Results 
The analysis identifies four principal dynamics: 
(1) Attribution Dilution 
The presence of synthetic media complicates the identification of the actor responsible 
for content creation and dissemination. 
(2) Evidentiary Instability 
Digital artifacts can no longer be presumed authentic without technical validation. 
(3) Scalability of Deception 
Generative AI enables large-scale production of fraudulent content with minimal cost. 
(4) Psychological Credibility 
Deepfakes exploit cognitive biases, increasing victim susceptibility. 
Operational Typology: 
Voice Cloning Fraud — financial deception — low detection threshold 
Synthetic Video Extortion — coercion — high psychological impact 
Identity Simulation — reputational harm — attribution complexity 
Hybrid Attacks — multi-platform deployment — rapid dissemination 
These patterns demonstrate that deepfake-enabled crime is structurally distinct from 
traditional fraud. 
 
5. Discussion 
The findings support the hypothesis that generative AI introduces 
evidentiary distortion rather than doctrinal transformation. 
Mens rea remains the central criterion for criminal liability. However, the inference of 
intent must rely on convergent evidence beyond synthetic artifacts. Communications, 
financial transactions, access logs, and behavioral patterns become essential 
corroborative elements. 
The study rejects any deterministic interpretation of algorithmic outputs. Artificial 
intelligence does not generate intent; it mediates representation. Therefore, liability 
must remain anchored in human conduct. 
The concept of algorithmic attribution provides a structured approach to resolving 
evidentiary ambiguity. By separating technological generation from human intent, 
courts can preserve doctrinal coherence while adapting to technological realities. 
 
6. Limitations 
The study is limited by reliance on secondary sources and the relative 
novelty of large-scale judicial treatment of deepfake evidence. 
Additionally, rapid technological evolution may alter the characteristics of synthetic 
media, requiring continuous doctrinal adaptation. 
Future research should include empirical case analysis, forensic benchmarking, and 
quantitative assessment of detection accuracy. 
 
7. Conclusions 
Generative AI represents a significant transformation in the evidentiary 
environment of criminal law. 
Deepfake technologies introduce structural challenges in attribution, reliability, and 
procedural fairness. However, they do not alter the normative foundations of criminal 
liability. 
The proposed model of algorithmic attribution offers a robust framework for 
distinguishing between synthetic outputs and human agency. 
Effective legal responses require: 
(1) enhanced evidentiary standards 
(2) forensic validation protocols 
(3) procedural transparency 
(4) interdisciplinary integration between law and technology 
Absent these safeguards, the risk of wrongful attribution and evidentiary distortion will 
increase substantially.

dc.description: Internet of Things (IoT)-powered smart home solutions are increasingly prevalent. As a result, they are significantly altering how we live today. Due to device heterogeneity, resource constraints, user awareness, and other factors, the systems that connect the Internet of Things (IoT) are themselves connected to other devices, making phishing attacks one of the most significant hazards in smart homes. Phishing undermines the privacy, security, and integrity of smart ecosystems by exploiting a user's trust through phony emails, voice squatting, URLs, among others. Since the current security techniques are insufficient, this study aim is to create a new tool based on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques to check and detect phishing attacks on smart home systems. This study makes use of enron dataset from Kaggle which contains a total of 33,715 email samples. Data pre-processing was carried out to extract relevant features and attributes from the dataset. The phishector.py script provides a command line interface for processing emails and obtaining predictions. The model was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and FI-score as performance metrics. From the obtained results, bagged decision tree model shows a 99.94% accuracy, precision 99.8%, F1-score, 99.94%, and recall, 100% while Adobos a 97.98% accuracy, precision 96.23%, F1-score, 98.08%, and recall, 100%. The study's result has further demonstrated how the suggested methods can be applied to detect phishing assaults in smart homes and shield linked smart devices from cyberattacks.

INTRODUCTION 
Over the past few decades, there has been a substantial 
advancement in the ability of networked devices across 
numerous users and industries to access and use the internet. 
These days, practically every modern activity involves the use 
of Internet-related services. In recent years, human lifestyles 
have become increasingly dependent on Internet of Things 
(IoT) services. This technology is being used to create a fully 
automated environment, or at the very least, efforts are being 
made to do so (George et al., 2024; Omar et al., 2024). IoT is 
a solution that makes it possible for people and things to be 
continuously and globally connected using any network or 
service (Zorgati et al., 2022). It was initially used to automate 
individual homes for more comfort and convenience, and it is 
now being expanded to build smart cities. The use of Internet 
of Things (IoT) devices to remotely control and automate 
household appliances and other equipment in order to 
enhance residents' quality of life is known as smart home 
technology. It is made up of smart devices connected by a 
router, including a smart thermostat, lights, security camera, 
Google Home, Alexa from Amazon, and smart locks. (George 
et al., 2024). In addition to encouraging environmental 
cleanliness and helping to create intelligent, sustainable 
communities, smart homes have a big impact on 
environmental sustainability. Increased comfort, a variety of 
energy sources, and housing options that are available to 
everybody are advantages of these technologies (Tetteh, & 
Amponsah, 2020). The latest wave of home automation is 
about more than just convenience. Smart homes can increase 
energy efficiency and reduce utility costs by automating tasks 
like lighting, temperature management, and security systems. 
However, due to continuous technology improvements, smart 
houses are anticipated to have a significant impact on the 
future of comfortable and efficient living (Allifah & 
Zualkernan, 2022). 
While smart homes offer convenience and automation, there 
are significant security and integration challenges. Smart 
homes can be complex systems with many devices, sensors, 
and services. This complexity may make it difficult to 
monitor security and identify intruders (SH2 study). 
Cyberattacks continue to be largely successful due to human 
mistake and home users' lack of awareness of security threats 
in smart homes (Gaber et al., 2024). Effective smart home 
security requires collaboration between internet service 
providers, device manufacturers, and homeowners. A 2022 
survey found that 40.3% of smart homes worldwide had five 
or more internet-connected devices, and 40.8% of families 
had at least one item that may harm the entire house. The 
majority of house users may not be aware of the cyber threats 
connected to smart-home devices or may not know how to 
properly protect them. Users are now viewed as one of the 
weak points in the cyber risk chain as a result of this (Allifah 
& Zualkernan, 2022). Because many consumers lack the 
knowledge required to correctly configure IoT devices, weak 
passwords, unpatched firmware, out-of-date software, and 
other security weaknesses are common entry points for 
attackers (Wan et al., 2020). 
A significant risk is posed by the security issues present in 
smart home environments, such as the usage of weak default 
passwords, unencrypted data transmission, sporadic firmware 
updates, and vulnerabilities in third-party applications. 
Regulatory loopholes further make matters worse because

there are no uniform security standards for IoT devices like

the primary problems with smart home devices is the absence 
of clear security guidelines from manufacturers. It might be 
difficult to ensure that smart home gadgets can all operate 
securely together because they are often made by multiple 
manufacturers and use different communication protocols 
(George et al., 2024). The authentication and encryption 
methods used to thwart infiltration attempts are unable to 
keep up with the fast changes in security protocols made by 
various vendors. Other systems are susceptible to security 
breaches if a smart home system has been exploited (Trim & 
Lee, 2023) The fact that there are currently no established 
security standards for smart home devices and that security 
features might differ greatly between manufacturers and 
products is another key security concern. Smart home systems 
are now a threat to data security, privacy, and an increase in 
attackers due to all of the aforementioned issues. As new 
security flaws emerge, smart homes have grown more 
unstable and susceptible (Kavallieratos et al. 2019). 
In order to protect smart home systems from hackers and 
enhance system dependability, a powerful and reliable 
intrusion detection system is therefore required. Several 
reviews and intrusion detection techniques have been carried 
out in the past years. (George et al., 2024). provided extensive 
survey that gives a full picture of security issues in IoT-
enabled smart homes. Its main contribution is a dual-focused 
research that details the particular vulnerabilities of common 
smart home devices and looks at threats across the typical 
four-layer IoT architecture. The process, which synthesizes a 
variety of risks and countermeasures, is a conventional 
literature review. Important conclusions include the necessity 
of layered defenses, the dangers of device heterogeneity, and 
the crucial role of user awareness.  By incorporating 
cybersecurity awareness into the Trust in Technology Model 
(TTM), (Alshammari & Al-Mamary, 2025) investigates the 
factors influencing the adoption of AI-driven smart home 
technologies. Using a quantitative survey and structural 
equation modeling, the study concludes that a user's overall 
inclination to trust technology enhances institution-based 
trust, which in turn fosters trust in particular devices. The 
user's cybersecurity awareness and this particular trust both 
greatly increase the intention to adopt these devices, and this 
intention is a strong predictor of deep, advanced usage. In 
order to accelerate the adoption of smart home technologies, 
the authors suggest that building confidence through 
institutional assurances and raising public cybersecurity 
knowledge are essential tactics. They provide important 
insights for regional politicians and technology innovators. 
Schiller et al., (2023) developed an approach to improving 
IoT network security using autonomous, swarm-based 
penetration testing, in which IoT devices proactively check 
other devices in the same network for weaknesses. The 
authors compared a conventional linear penetration testing 
algorithm with two swarm-based methods—a queue-based 
algorithm and a nature-inspired Particle Swarm Optimization 
(PSO) algorithm—across both small smart home (30 devices) 
and large smart building (250 devices) scales using a custom 
network simulator (CyberSim-SwarmIoT). The findings 
showed that swarm-based techniques, especially the PSO 
algorithm, found vulnerabilities much more quickly and 
thoroughly than linear techniques. Over time, the PSO 
approach achieved the highest unique vulnerability detection 
rate while outperforming the queue-based method in terms of 
computational efficiency. The study concludes that using 
coordinated swarms of IoT devices for autonomous 
penetration testing can significantly increase security 
awareness and vulnerability identification in smart 
environments, providing a proactive defense mechanism that 
makes use of already-existing network resources. With an 
emphasis on smart wall pads—central control devices with 
displays that retain substantial user data, Kim et al., (2024) 
developed a four-stage forensic methodology for smart home 
environments. Data gathering by network packet capture, 
vulnerability exploitation, serial port access, and chip-off 
techniques, data analysis to extract user-related artifacts, data 
validation for legal proof, and forensic preparation to identify 
device specs are all part of the methodology. By successfully 
extracting forensic artifacts like user phone numbers, linked 
device lists, visitor video thumbnails, security event logs, and 
voice memos, the authors validate their method on testbeds 
from three vendors (Samsung, Kocom, and Commax). This 
shows that wall pads are rich sources of digital evidence and 
that giving their analysis priority can improve efficiency in 
smart home forensic investigations. 
The important security issues of node capture attacks in IoT-
based smart home systems was proposed by (Asghar et al., 
2023). The authors first do a security analysis of current user-
authentication schemes, finding that many of them are 
susceptible to such physical attacks and lack crucial security 
features. They respond by putting up a brand-new, 
lightweight user-authentication system made specially to fend 
off node capture assaults. The suggested method includes a 
number of security characteristics, including forward secrecy, 
mutual authentication between the user, gateway, and smart 
devices, user anonymity through the use of dynamic 
temporary identities, and protection against location 
monitoring. Formal techniques, such as BAN logic to 
demonstrate mutual authentication and session key agreement 
and the ProVerif tool to confirm the confidentiality of key 
parameters and authentication events, are used to thoroughly 
validate the security of the suggested scheme. Additionally, 
compared to a number of cutting-edge protocols, a 
performance analysis shows that the scheme is 
computationally and communication ally economical, 
making it appropriate for IoT devices with limited resources. 
The study concludes that the suggested plan effectively 
reduces the vulnerabilities found while keeping overhead to a 
minimum. 
Javed et al., (2024) proposed a revolutionary, decentralized 
intrusion detection system (IDS) that is integrated straight 
into a smart thermostat. The implementation and quantization 
of a Cat Boost machine learning model for on-device 
intrusion detection, a technique not natively supported by 
existing microcontroller machine learning libraries; the 
creation of a unique dataset (IDSH) based on features 
extractable directly from a microcontroller (ESP32) using the 
lip library, as opposed to traditional gateway-captured traffic; 
and a thorough performance evaluation contrasting the 
suggested Cat Boost-based IDS against an XGBoost-based 
IDS are some of the major contributions. In terms of 
accuracy, inference speed, and program storage efficiency, 
the system beat the XGBoost benchmark, demonstrating the 
viability of directly implementing a reliable, lightweight IDS 
on resource-constrained IoT devices to improve protection 
against frequent intrusions. Kavallieratos et al., (2019) 
offered a thorough methodology for threat analysis and 
modeling. The main component of their strategy is utilizing 
an existing smart home reference architecture to conduct a 
thorough threat analysis using Microsoft's threat modeling 
tool and the STRIDE method, concentrating on the 
communication and physical perspectives across six smart 
home scenarios of varying complexity. The investigation

However, as the IoT ecosystem continues to grow, intrusion 
such as phishing attack needs more attention in order to 
protect user data, privacy, and prevent more significant issues 
(Deldar & Abadi 2023). Phishing is a gift that may cause 
significant harm, and the proliferation of smart home 
technologies has significantly increased their vulnerability to 
cyber threats. Phishing using voice command or email takes 
advantage of user trust (Gupta et al., 2018). In order to obtain 
unauthorized access to smart devices or their networks, 
attackers pose as reliable parties. Attackers might, for 
instance, utilize voice squatting to steal data from unprotected 
devices or activate home assistants with similar-sounding 
utterances (Zhang et al., 2021) Therefore, for threat avoidance 
and suitable intrusion detection techniques, new techniques 
and outcomes are essential. Recently developed machine 
learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques are being 
used for intrusion detection, categorizing anomalies in the 
network, and discouraging it. Convolutional neural networks 
(CNNs), deep belief networks (DBNs), recurrent neural 
networks (RNNs), and restricted Boltzmann machines 
(RBMs) are among the networks found in DL (Sabeenian et 
al., 2020; Almutairi, & Alshargabi, 2022). But, the security 
measures in place are insufficient. The authentication and 
encryption methods used to stop phishing assaults are unable 
to keep up with the advancements. Additionally, IoT devices 
lack the resources necessary to combat phishing assaults. In 
multi-device linked environments, traditional intrusion 
detection systems (IDSs) are unable to keep up with 
cybercriminals' rapid-fire attacks (Trim & Lee, 2023). The 
lack of uniform security procedures across manufacturers is 
one of the main issues with smart home appliances. An 
advanced solution that can use ML and DL to detect phishing 
assaults on smart home systems in real time and turn them 
into anti-phishing systems is needed. Hence, this study aims 
to develop and evaluate a machine-learning-based phishing 
detection model for smart-home environments. 
 
MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Using machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) 
techniques, this study developed a dedicated tool to identify 
phishing attempts in smart home systems. In order to 
effectively identify phishing attempts across heterogeneous 
IoT devices, the methodology combines supervised and 
unsupervised learning algorithms to assess data from network 
traffic, device logs, and user interactions. While unsupervised 
DL models, like auto encoders, use anomaly detection to 
identify new threats, supervised ML models, like random 
forests, will categorize existing phishing trends. Lightweight 
model architectures and edge computing were used to support 
the resource limitations of IoT devices, guaranteeing 
interoperability with various protocols like Zigbee and Wi-Fi. 
Federated learning and other privacy-preserving strategies 
will be used to reduce data exposure and boost user 
confidence. Data from simulated smart home environments 
was gathered, models are trained and optimized, and 
performance is assessed using metrics like accuracy and false 
positive rate. Virtual machine (VM) running Kali Linux, an 
open-source Linux distribution for penetration testing 
primarily used by cybersecurity experts and black hats, to 
simulate a phishing attack scenario in order to gain a better 
understanding of how phishing attacks operate. 
 
Phishing Detection Tool 
Using Python libraries such as numpy for numerical 
computation, pandas for data manipulation, BeatifulSoup for 
HTML parsing, scikit-learn for machine learning models, and 
TensorFlow for the deep learning model, and four the 
phishing detection tool were used which are listed below: 
i. Kali Linux VM: A virtual machine hosting a 2023 
version of the Kali Linux operating system. 
ii. Koadic: An open-source windows operating 
system post-exploitation tool installed using the 
Kali Linux VM terminal with the command sudo 
apt install Koadic. 
iii. Two Dummy Gmail Accounts: Two Gmail accounts 
were created, one to function as the victim’s email 
address and the other to function as the attacker’s 
email address. 
iv. Network: The VM was configured using an NAT 
bridged adapter network to simulate connectivity 
with the VM and base windows OS as two different 
machines with different IP addresses. 
 
The Phishing Simulation was Carried out in the Following 
Steps 
i. After creating two fictitious Gmail accounts to act

ii. In order to trick the victim into downloading my 
payload and granting access to their computer, an 
Apache server running the command sudo apt 
install apache2 was used to host a dummy webpage. 
HTML and CSS were utilized to create a fake 
smart-home company webpage. 
iii. A payload named ‘security_update.bat’ to echo the 
IP address and the port where stager is hosted on 
the Kali Linux VM and both my dummy webpage 
and the payload were hosted on the apache server. 
iv. A straightforward phishing email sample was

The Model Architecture 
The basic idea behind hybridization is to improve detection 
performance by using machine learning to choose meaningful 
characteristics and/or classify the produced data and deep 
learning to automatically extract complicated features from 
phishing-related data. The following processing steps provide

Data Collection 
Gathering information from the smart home network and the 
digital services that its residents utilize is the first step. The 
home router or IoT gateway can be used to monitor pertinent 
network traffic. The data used for this study was the enron 
dataset from Kaggle which contains a total of 33,715 email 
samples in a .csv format with four columns namely 
“Message”, “Subject”, “Spam/Ham” and “Date”. The 
“Message” column contains the full content of the email 
sample, including its headers, body, and metadata, while the

Noise, missing values, duplicate entries, and mismatched

This is the hybridization process's first significant step. Deep

dc.description:
Background: The increasing use of smartphones has been accompanied by the growing misuse of mobile devices in cybercrime, making mobile forensics essential for identifying, acquiring, recovering, and analyzing digital evidence. However, standardized mobile forensic investigation models for field implementation remain limited. The Harmonized Mobile Forensic Investigation Process Model (HMFIPM) has been proposed as a structured investigation model, but its empirical implementation in an accredited forensic laboratory environment remains underexplored.


Objective: This study aims to empirically validate the implementation of HMFIPM as a structured process model for Android mobile forensic investigations within an ISO/IEC 17025-accredited Digital Forensics Laboratory.


Methods: This study applied a descriptive and implementation-based approach. Descriptive analysis was conducted through examiner interviews, while implementation analysis was performed by applying the HMFIPM stages to a Samsung SM-A075F device using Full File System extraction with Cellebrite UFED and Android Live extraction with MD.


Results: All HMFIPM stages were successfully implemented and mapped to the mobile forensic workflow in the laboratory environment. The model supported a structured, documented, and evaluable investigation process. Differences in artifact recovery were primarily caused by tool-to-method compatibility and application data architecture rather than by limitations of the HMFIPM model. Cellebrite UFED using Full File System acquisition produced more complete artifacts, while MD using Android Live extraction obtained partial application artifacts.

Conclusion: HMFIPM is feasible as a standardized framework for Android mobile forensic investigation. However, the feedback mechanism requires refinement. This study proposes an additional data acquisition feedback path alongside the existing analysis feedback path, allowing examiners to revisit the acquisition stage when new investigative needs arise.

Mobile	forensics	(MF)	is	a	branch	of	digital	forensics	(DF)	that	focuses	on	the	process	of	
acquiring,	recovering,	and	analyzing	data	from	mobile	devices	such	as	smartphones	and	tablets.	
This	field	plays	a	crucial	role	in	assisting	investigators	in	uncovering	digitally	stored	electronic	
evidence	 that	 can	 be	 used	 in	 law	 enforcement	 processes	(Fukami	 et	 al.,	 2021).	 However,	
technological	advancements,	operating	system	complexity,	and	variations	in	extraction	methods	
pose	challenges	for	investigators	in	maintaining	data	integrity	and	ensuring	that	each	stage	of	the	
process	complies	with	digital	forensic	laboratory	standards,	such	as	ISO/IEC	17025.	
In	line	with	these	needs,	research	conducted	by	Arafat	Al-Dhaqm	et	al.	(2021)	proposed	
the	 Harmonized	 Mobile	 Forensic	 Investigation	 Process	 Model	 (HMFIPM)	 as	 a	 framework	 that	
integrates	various	structured	mobile	forensic	investigation	processes	(Banesinh,	2025;	Haluszka	
&	Mansour,	2023;	Şen	&	Artuner,	2025).	The	study	recommended	that	the	HMFIPM	be	tested	and	
validated	in	real-world	contexts	to	ensure	its	effectiveness	and	compatibility	with	current	forensic	
practices.	 Based	 on	 this	 recommendation,	 the	 present	 research	 was	 conducted	 to	 validate	 the	
HMFIPM	on	Android	devices	in	a	Digital	Forensics	Laboratory	using	two	primary	extraction	tools,	
Cellebrite	UFED	and	MD,	within	an	ISO/IEC	17025-accredited	laboratory	environment	(Hamad	&	
Eleyan,	2022).	
This	research	is	designed	to	address	several	primary	research	questions,	namely	how	the	
validation	process	of	the	Harmonized	Mobile	Forensic	Investigation	Process	Model	(HMFIPM)	is	
implemented	 on	 Android	 devices	 in	 a	 Digital	 Forensics	 Laboratory	 environment,	 and	 how	 the	
verification	results	demonstrate	the	feasibility	of	the	HMFIPM	as	a	standardized	mobile	forensic	
investigation	process	model.	In	line	with	these	research	questions,	the	general	objective	of	this	
study	 is	 to	 validate	 the	 HMFIPM	 as	 a	 mobile	 forensic	 investigation	 model	 for	 Android	 devices	
within	 an	 ISO/IEC	 17025-standardized	 Digital	 Forensics	 Laboratory	 environment.	 Specifically,	
this	research	aims	to	assess	the	applicability	of	each	procedure	and	stage	in	the	HMFIPM	within	
the	 context	 of	 an	 actual	 investigation	 and	 to	 evaluate	 the	 consistency	 and	 reliability	 of	 digital	
evidence	extraction	results	through	the	use	of	two	different	forensic	tools,	namely	Cellebrite	UFED	
and	MD.	
The	 benefit	 of	 this	 research	 is	 that	 it	 provides	 empirical	 validation	 of	 the	 conceptual	
HMFIPM	 on	 Android	 devices	 and	 contributes	 to	 narrowing	 the	 research	 gap	 in	 Indonesia	
regarding	 the	 validation	 of	 mobile	 forensic	 investigation	 models.	 Meanwhile,	 the	 scope	 of	 this	
research	is	focused	on	analyzing	data	extracted	from	Android	devices	that	have	been	verified	as	a	
ground	 truth	 dataset	 by	 forensic	 analysts	 in	 a	 digital	 forensics	 laboratory.	 This	 research	
specifically	 uses	 a	 Samsung	 Android	 device	 as	 the	 primary	 object	 of	 investigation,	 with	 the	
extraction	 process	 conducted	 using	 two	 forensic	 tools,	 Cellebrite	 UFED	 and	MD,	 to	 ensure	 the	
validity	and	reliability	of	the	investigation	results.	
	
METHOD	
The	 data	 analysis	 technique	 in	 this	 study	 was	 carried	 out	 through	 a	 descriptive	 and	
implementation-based	 approach	 to	 the	 application	 of	 the	 Harmonized	 Mobile	 Forensic	
Investigation	 Process	 Model	 (HMFIPM)	 in	 mobile	 forensic	 investigations	 of	 Android	 devices.	
Qualitative	analysis	was	conducted	based	on	the	results	of	interviews	with	examiners	and	digital	
forensic	investigators	at	the	Digital	Forensic	Laboratory	to	obtain	information	related	to	mobile	
forensic	 investigation	 practices	 in	 the	 field.	 This	 analysis	 was	 used	 to	 determine	 the	 Android	
device	 used	 as	 a	 test	 object,	 compile	 the	 research	 dataset,	 select	 an	 acquisition	 method,	 and	
understand	 the	 implementation	 of	 each	 HMFIPM	 stage	 in	 the	 digital	 forensic	 investigation	
process.	 The	 model	 implementation	 analysis	 was	 conducted	 through	 the	 application	 of	 the	
HMFIPM	stages	in	the	mobile	forensic	investigation	process	on	the	device,	where	the	results	of	
the	 acquisition	 and	 analysis	 of	 digital	 artifacts	 were	 used	 to	 evaluate	 the	 applicability	 of	 each	
HMFIPM	 stage,	 identify	 the	 dynamics	 of	 the	 investigation	 process,	 and	 assess	 the	 need	 for	
feedback-based	 improvements	 derived	 from	 the	 investigation	 results	 obtained	 during	
implementation.

The	 stages	 of	 this	 research	 followed	 the	 Harmonized	 Mobile	 Forensic	 Investigation	
Process	Model	(HMFIPM)	workflow,	starting	with	the	preparation	stage,	i.e.,	preparing	the	device	
and	forensic	investigation	environment	by	ensuring	the	readiness	of	the	tools	and	the	Android	
device	 as	 the	 research	 object.	 Next,	 the	 preservation	 stage	 was	 carried	 out	 to	 maintain	 the	
integrity	of	the	evidence	through	an	initial	condition	assessment	of	the	device,	network	isolation	
(Airplane	Mode	and	disabling	Wi-Fi	and	Bluetooth),	as	well	as	lawful	device	access	and	enabling	
Developer	 Options	 as	 prerequisites	 for	 acquisition.	 The	 data	 acquisition	 stage	 was	 conducted	
using	 the	 physical	 extraction	 method	 to	 obtain	 comprehensive	 data,	 including	 both	 active	 and	
residual	data.	The	acquired	data	were	then	processed	during	the	examination	stage	through	the	
parsing	 of	 artifacts,	 such	 as	 system	 logs,	 metadata,	 and	 application	 artifacts,	 for	 structured	
analysis.	 The	 analysis	 stage	 focused	 on	 interpreting	 digital	 artifacts	 to	 identify	 patterns	 and	
relevant	 information	 based	 on	 the	 ground	 truth	 dataset,	 which	 was	 subsequently	 evaluated	 to	
ensure	data	validity	and	sufficiency.	This	process	incorporated	a	feedback	mechanism	during	the	
reporting	stage,	namely	examination	feedback	for	data	quality	control	and	analysis	feedback	for	
analyst	quality	control.	The	final	stage	was	presentation,	i.e.,	presenting	the	investigation	results	
in	the	form	of	systematic,	transparent,	and	accountable	reports	and	visualizations.	
	
Data	Analysis	Techniques	
The	data	in	this	study	were	analyzed	descriptively	and	interpretatively	based	on	the	result	
of	examiner	interviews	and	the	implementation	of	the	HMFIPM	stages.	The	analysis	focused	on	
assessing	the	suitability	and	applicability	of	HMFIPM	in	Android	mobile	forensic	investigations,	
identifying	 process	 dynamics	 during	 acquisition	 and	 analysis,	 and	 formulating	 feedback-based	
improvements	based	on	the	findings	obtained	during	implementation.

Research	Results	
Simulation	of	HMFIPM	Model	Investigation	Implementation	
The	 simulation	 of	 the	 HMFIPM	 model	 in	 the	 Digital	 Forensics	 Lab	 began	 with	
implementing	the	first	stage	of	the	HMFIPM	model:	preparation.	Previous	research	explained	that	
the	preparation	stage	involves	isolating	the	mobile	device	to	achieve	a	forensically	sound	state	
and	prevent	data	alteration	on	the	mobile	device.	In	this	study,	isolation	was	performed	when	the	
investigator	 submitted	 the	 evidence	 for	 extraction	 to	 the	 forensic	 lab	 officer	 on	 duty	 at	 the	
reception	counter.	The	officer	checked	the	condition	of	the	evidence,	ensuring	that	Airplane	Mode	
was	activated	and	that	the	SIM	and	memory	cards	had	been	removed	to	maintain	the	status	quo.	
The	officer	then	recorded	detailed	information,	physically	documented	the	phone	and	the	time	of	
submission	 in	 the	 chain-of-custody	 form,	 prepared	 a	 handover	 report	 containing	 the	 evidence	
examination	number,	and	issued	a	receipt	letter	(STP).	Subsequently,	the	documents	and	evidence	
were	handed	over	to	the	examiner.
